Gibeah
GIB-ee-uh
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Gibe'ah (H1390), "hill, height" (from geva, "hill"). A town in the territory of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem; "Gibeah of Saul," the hometown and royal seat of King Saul.

📖 Biblical Definition

Gibeah was a town in the tribal territory of Benjamin, infamous as the scene of one of the darkest episodes in the book of Judges and later notable as the hometown and capital of King Saul. The dark episode comes at the end of Judges, in the days when "there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25). A Levite and his concubine, traveling, lodged at Gibeah; the wicked men of the city surrounded the house and, in an outrage echoing the sin of Sodom, abused the concubine through the night until she died (Judg 19). The Levite's gruesome summons to the tribes provoked a civil war in which the tribe of Benjamin, defending the men of Gibeah, was nearly annihilated (Judg 20). Gibeah thus stands as a monument to the moral chaos of the period of the judges — what Israel became when every man did what was right in his own eyes, when even the covenant people sank to the depravity of Sodom. Later, Gibeah became the hometown and royal residence of Saul, the first king of Israel (1 Sam 10:26; 11:4; "Gibeah of Saul," 1 Sam 15:34), so that the town's name is bound to the tragic king whose reign began in promise and ended in rejection. The prophet Hosea later recalled Gibeah's ancient wickedness as a byword for the depth of Israel's corruption: "they have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah" (Hos 9:9; 10:9). Gibeah is a sober place: it testifies to how far a covenant people can fall when they cast off the fear of God, and it reminds the reader that the human heart, left to itself, is capable of Sodom's sins even within the visible people of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A town of Benjamin; scene of the outrage against the Levite's concubine and the near-destruction of Benjamin (Judg 19-20), a monument to the moral chaos when every man did what was right in his own eyes; later the hometown and capital of King Saul (1 Sam 10:26).

GIBEAH, proper noun. Hebrew Gibe'ah (H1390), "hill, height"; a town in Benjamin, north of Jerusalem.

Scene of the outrage against the Levite's concubine, echoing the sin of Sodom (Judg 19).

The outrage provoked civil war and the near-annihilation of Benjamin (Judg 20).

A monument to the chaos of the judges: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25).

Later the hometown and royal seat of Saul, "Gibeah of Saul" (1 Sam 10:26; 15:34); recalled by Hosea as a byword for corruption (Hos 9:9).

📖 Key Scripture

Judges 19:22 — "Now as they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, certain sons of Belial, beset the house round about... saying, Bring forth the man that came into thine house, that we may know him."

Judges 21:25 — "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

1 Samuel 10:26 — "And Saul also went home to Gibeah; and there went with him a band of men, whose hearts God had touched."

Hosea 9:9 — "They have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah: therefore he will remember their iniquity, he will visit their sins."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Gibeah is corrupted when its horror is read as mere ancient barbarism rather than a mirror of the human heart, when the "every man did right in his own eyes" refrain is missed, or when the depravity within the covenant people is explained away.

expand to see more

Distant-barbarism dismissal. The outrage at Gibeah is so horrifying that modern readers may distance themselves from it as the barbarism of a primitive age, far removed from civilized people. The book of Judges intends the opposite effect: Gibeah was not a pagan city but a town of the covenant people Israel, and its men sank to the very sin of Sodom. The refrain that frames the episode — "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25) — is the diagnosis: when the fear of God is cast off and each person becomes his own law, even God's own people are capable of Sodom's depravity. Gibeah is a mirror, not a museum piece: it shows what the human heart, including the religious heart, becomes when it throws off God's law.

Gibeah has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is its testimony to the depth of human depravity even within the visible people of God, and the chaos that results when "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25). Our own age, which exalts the autonomy of the individual will and the right of each person to define right and wrong for himself, is the days of Gibeah in modern dress. The remedy then and now is the same: the King, the fear of God, and the rule of His Word over the autonomous self.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

A town of Benjamin; scene of the outrage against the Levite's concubine and Benjamin's near-destruction (Judg 19-20); a monument to the chaos when every man did right in his own eyes; later Saul's hometown and capital (1 Sam 10:26).
